title: Theoretical Investigation of Oxygen-Vacancy Diffusion in SrTiO$_3$ using Neural Network Potentials
authors: Kazutaka Nishiguchi, Ryota Yamamoto, Seiichiro Ten-no
abstract: Oxygen-vacancy formation and diffusion play important roles in determining the electronic and atomic transport properties of SrTiO$_3$ (STO). Accurate analysis of such point defects requires sufficiently large-scale and long-time molecular dynamics (MD) simulations; however, direct investigations of oxygen-vacancy dynamics using {\it ab initio} MD (AIMD) based on density functional theory (DFT) are limited to relatively small systems and short time scales because of their high computational cost. In this study, we develop a neural network potential (NNP) for pristine and oxygen-deficient STO using a reference dataset generated from AIMD simulations. The trained NNP model accurately reproduces the DFT reference energies, atomic forces, and virials for both pristine STO and STO containing an oxygen vacancy. The NNP also reproduces the supercell-size dependence of the total energies and oxygen-vacancy formation energies, including the formation energy extrapolated to the dilute limit. Large-scale and long-time MD simulations using the NNP (NNP-MD) are then performed to investigate oxygen-vacancy diffusion. The resulting oxygen-vacancy diffusion coefficients show substantially better agreement with experimental data than those obtained from conventional classical MD simulations. An Arrhenius analysis yields an oxygen-vacancy migration enthalpy of 0.64 eV, in close agreement with the experimental value of 0.67 eV. These results demonstrate that NNPs trained on first-principles data provide an accurate and computationally efficient framework for investigating defect formation and long-time vacancy transport in perovskite oxides.

infographic.key_insight: A neural network potential trained on first-principles data can accurately reproduce oxygen-vacancy energetics and enable long-timescale diffusion simulations in SrTiO3.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a practical route to predict defect transport in perovskite oxides with near-DFT accuracy at a fraction of the cost, aiding materials design for electronic and ionic functionality.
method: Trained an NNP on AIMD/DFT reference data for pristine and oxygen-deficient SrTiO3.
Validated energies, forces, virials, and vacancy formation energies across supercell sizes.
Used large-scale NNP-MD and Arrhenius analysis to extract vacancy diffusion coefficients and migration enthalpy.
infographic.evidence_signal: The NNP matched DFT reference properties and produced a vacancy migration enthalpy of 0.64 eV, close to the experimental 0.67 eV.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on the quality and coverage of the DFT training set, so unusual defect states or compositions outside the sampled space may require retraining.
infographic.paper_title: Theoretical Investigation of Oxygen-Vacancy Diffusion in SrTiO$_3$ using Neural Network Potentials

title: Modelling the dynamics of the martensitic transformation in Ni$_2$MnGa with machine-learning force-fields
authors: Markus E. Gruner, Yulia Klunnikova, Mike J. Bruckhoff, Konstatin P. Skokov, Olga N. Miroshkina
abstract: The martensitic transformations in stoichiometric Ni$_2$MnGa and related Heusler alloys are governed by a delicate interplay between electronic structure, magnetism, and lattice dynamics. While density functional theory (DFT) has successfully mapped the energy landscape of modulated martensites, it remains computationally prohibitive for capturing finite-temperature dynamics across relevant length and time scales. Here, we bridge this gap by constructing DFT-trained machine-learning force-fields (ML-FF) interpolated from ab initio molecular dynamics. We demonstrate that ML-FF trained on DFT data can reproduce key features of Ni$_2$MnGa, including the soft TA$_2$ phonon and a preference for nanotwinned martensites. Using classical molecular dynamics simulations, we explore the impact of adaptive nanotwinning on the austenite-martensite transition, which facilitates the dynamics of both, forward and backward transformation. We demonstrate, that the negative twin boundary energy along the entire transformations path predicted by DFT for $T=0$, supports the formation of ordered modulated martensites at finite temperatures. Our results pave the way for large-scale simulations of magnetic shape memory alloys with near-DFT accuracy.

infographic.key_insight: DFT-trained machine-learning force fields can reproduce the martensitic dynamics of Ni2MnGa, including soft phonons and nanotwinned modulated martensites, at scales inaccessible to direct DFT.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables near-DFT-accuracy simulation of magnetic shape-memory alloys across finite temperature and larger time scales, supporting design of faster and more reliable actuation materials.
method: Train machine-learning force fields on ab initio molecular dynamics data from DFT.
Run classical molecular dynamics to capture austenite-martensite transformation pathways.
Analyze phonons, twin boundaries, and nanotwin-mediated transformation behavior.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that the ML-FF reproduces key DFT features of Ni2MnGa, including the TA2 soft phonon and a preference for nanotwinned martensites, while also matching the predicted negative twin boundary energy along the transformation path.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy depends on the quality and coverage of the DFT training data, so unseen transformation pathways or compositions may require retraining or validation.
infographic.paper_title: Modelling the dynamics of the martensitic transformation in Ni$_2$MnGa with machine-learning force-fields

title: Comprehensive Workflow for Uncertainty-Aware Ionic Liquid Solvent Discovery
authors: Alexander Lobo, Urvi Awasthi, Leonid Zhukov
abstract: Designing synthesizable materials with targeted properties remains one of the central objectives in materials sciences. Ionic liquids (ILs) are well suited to this goal due to their "tunability", where physical and chemical properties can be precisely customized by modifying their molecular structure, specifically by varying the combination of cations and anions. At the same time, current data-driven property models for ionic liquids often degrade in scarce, noisy, and uneven data regimes, where measurements cover only a small fraction of chemical space and a limited range of thermodynamic conditions. This makes out-of-distribution screening brittle: even when point predictions look plausible, it is difficult to compare candidates consistently, quantify downstream implications, or trust rankings enough to guide molecular discovery. We present a property-prediction and optimal candidate selection workflow that treats data processing, deep learning modeling, and physics-based calculations as a coupled system, linking property prediction with uncertainty estimation and physics-based filtering. By tightening the link between predicted properties and the criteria used for down-selection, the workflow supports reliable out-of-distribution ranking and enables prioritization of previously untested ionic liquid candidates with favorable predicted trade-offs. We demonstrate the application of our workflow by designing novel ionic liquids for CO2 capture from flue gas, predicting their properties and selecting Pareto-optimal candidates based on CO2 solubility, IL viscosity and working capacity.

infographic.key_insight: A coupled property-prediction and physics-filtering workflow can rank unexplored ionic liquids more reliably by accounting for uncertainty in sparse, noisy, out-of-distribution data.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables faster, more trustworthy screening of synthesizable ionic liquids for CO2 capture by prioritizing candidates with favorable trade-offs in solubility, viscosity, and working capacity.
method: Process sparse and uneven ionic-liquid data for deep learning property prediction.
Estimate prediction uncertainty to support robust out-of-distribution screening and ranking.
Apply physics-based calculations and Pareto selection to filter candidates for CO2 capture.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports demonstration on novel ionic liquids for flue-gas CO2 capture, with candidate selection based on predicted CO2 solubility, viscosity, and working capacity.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may still be sensitive to data sparsity and measurement noise, so uncertainty estimates and rankings should be validated carefully before experimental follow-up.
infographic.paper_title: Comprehensive Workflow for Uncertainty-Aware Ionic Liquid Solvent Discovery

title: Accurately Generalizing Deep-Learning Hamiltonian Methods to Plane-Wave Density Functional Theory
authors: Chuntian Wu, Jiaxiang Li, Qiang Xu, Xuecheng Shao, Congwei Xie, Yu Xie
abstract: Deep neural networks that predict density functional theory (DFT) Hamiltonians from material structures offer a route to efficient electronic-structure calculations. However, extending localized atomic-orbital (AO) Hamiltonian learning to plane-wave (PW) calculations with hybrid functionals requires a compact AO representation that preserves the effects of nonlocal operators. Here we propose a projectability-guided construction of nonorthogonal AO Hamiltonians from a small, selected set of PW eigenstates and eigenvalues. High-projectability states are retained, and selected higher-energy states complete the AO subspace, avoiding an empirical shift and its arbitrary contribution to the learning targets. Because the construction uses PW eigenstates and eigenvalues, it incorporates nonlocal contributions present in the reference calculation without explicitly reconstructing their AO matrix elements. Benchmarks for MoS2 and sodium phases show accurate reproduction of PW bands with smaller AO bases than real-space reconstruction. The resulting PBE and HSE Hamiltonians can be learned by equivariant neural networks, connecting PW reference calculations with electronic-structure prediction. This approach broadens the range of PW DFT calculations available for AO Hamiltonian learning and enables compact, accurate training targets for developing more widely applicable electronic-structure models.

infographic.key_insight: A projectability-guided atomic-orbital construction lets deep-learning Hamiltonian models learn compact, accurate targets from plane-wave DFT, including hybrid-functional nonlocal effects.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables faster and more transferable electronic-structure prediction by bridging plane-wave reference calculations with equivariant neural Hamiltonian learning.
method: Select high-projectability plane-wave eigenstates to define the retained AO subspace.
Add selected higher-energy states to complete the basis without an empirical energy shift.
Build PBE/HSE AO Hamiltonians from PW eigenvalues/eigenstates, preserving nonlocal contributions implicitly.
infographic.evidence_signal: Benchmarks on MoS2 and sodium phases show the constructed AO Hamiltonians reproduce plane-wave band structures accurately with smaller bases than real-space reconstruction.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on careful state selection and projectability thresholds, which may affect robustness across more complex materials systems.
infographic.paper_title: Accurately Generalizing Deep-Learning Hamiltonian Methods to Plane-Wave Density Functional Theory

title: Composition-controlled optical fingerprints and anisotropy of self-trapped excitons in double perovskites
authors: Simone Grillo, Offir Zachs Maishlos, Liya Koren, Rotem Strassberg, Rachel Lifer, Edi Maizenberg
abstract: Double perovskites (DPs) offer a compositionally versatile platform for photocatalysis and optoelectronics, but their soft lattices favor strong exciton-phonon coupling and self-trapped excitons (STEs), which produce broad, red-shifted photoluminescence (PL). Here, we combine optical spectroscopy and ab initio calculations to study lead-free, Sb-doped Cs2BInCl6 nanocrystals with B-site alloying from Na to K. Alloying tunes the PL energy from about 2.48 to 2.70 eV, while absorption features near 3.8 eV remain nearly unchanged. Calculations reveal that Sb doping enables bright radiative recombination channels and delocalizes the excitonic wavefunction. We identify STEs responsible for the large PL red shift, associated with an upward shift of dopant-hybridized in-gap states. Na-to-K substitution selectively changes the STE lattice distortion, explaining why PL varies strongly with composition while absorption does not. Theory further predicts pronounced PL polarization anisotropy that reflects the STE wavefunction's spatial structure and depends on B-site composition. Time-resolved anisotropy measurements closely agree with these predictions, providing experimental fingerprints of the excitonic wavefunction and its evolution with alloying. Together, these results disentangle the roles of doping and alloying in lead-free DPs and establish polarization-resolved spectroscopy as a probe of STE wavefunctions.

infographic.key_insight: Sb doping in Na/K-alloyed Cs2BInCl6 double perovskite nanocrystals creates self-trapped excitons that strongly red-shift photoluminescence, while B-site composition selectively tunes the exciton lattice distortion and polarization anisotropy.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This work identifies composition knobs for tuning color output and exciton behavior in lead-free perovskites, useful for designing stable optoelectronic and photocatalytic materials.
method: Optical spectroscopy of Sb-doped Cs2BInCl6 nanocrystals across Na-to-K B-site alloying
Ab initio calculations of excitonic states, radiative channels, and lattice distortions
Time-resolved polarization-anisotropy measurements to test predicted wavefunction fingerprints
infographic.evidence_signal: PL shifts from about 2.48 to 2.70 eV while the absorption feature near 3.8 eV remains nearly unchanged, and measured anisotropy closely matches theory.
infographic.watch_item: The conclusions rely on nanocrystal composition control and model-dependent interpretation of exciton-phonon coupling, so broader material generalization may require additional validation.
infographic.paper_title: Composition-controlled optical fingerprints and anisotropy of self-trapped excitons in double perovskites

title: Learning from fracture: Teaching language models to design through physical experience
authors: Bo Ni
abstract: How can language models learn to optimize physical designs through experience? We introduce FracLearn, an experience-abstraction-generalization framework evaluated through a deliberately unfamiliar, Tetris-inspired fracture game. The model first proposes architectures and examines simulated fracture responses to accumulate experience. Abstraction organizes these observations into conditional principles linking reinforcement placement, crack evolution and load transfer, with supporting evidence and failure conditions. Generalization challenges the model to combine these principles in new architectures and surpass the earlier design record. Campaigns demonstrate progressive refinement and recovery through hypothesis revision, yielding a best composite score 11.0% above the experience-stage record. Fracture analyses connect improved performance to crack deflection and temporary trapping as toughening mechanisms, alongside greater residual load capacity. Learning occurs through external knowledge and decisions, without model-weight updates. This approach offers a route to scientific agents that turn computational experiments into reusable physical knowledge for materials discovery and engineering design.

infographic.key_insight: FracLearn teaches a language model to improve physical design decisions by turning simulated fracture experiences into reusable principles for better architecture generation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework suggests a path for materials and structural design agents that learn from experiments without retraining model weights, potentially speeding discovery of tougher, more efficient designs.
method: Generate candidate architectures in a fracture-based game environment.
Observe simulated fracture responses and abstract them into conditional design principles.
Generalize those principles to new designs and revise hypotheses through repeated campaigns.
infographic.evidence_signal: In evaluation, the best composite score exceeded the experience-stage record by 11.0%, with fracture analysis linking gains to crack deflection, temporary trapping, and higher residual load capacity.
infographic.watch_item: Results come from a deliberately unfamiliar game-like simulator, so transfer to real materials systems may require careful validation.
infographic.paper_title: Learning from fracture: Teaching language models to design through physical experience

title: Learning When to Transfer: Reinforcement Learning for Carbon-Footprint Modeling in New Manufacturing Domains
authors: Muhammad Umar Farooq, Daniel R. Cooper
abstract: Manufacturers often need to characterize a new material, process, or product before enough operating data are available to train reliable predictive models for this new, target domain. Existing manufacturing operations contain potentially useful knowledge to accelerate this characterization, but indiscriminate reuse of data from existing source domains can cause negative transfer in learning of the new, target domain when the manufacturing domains differ sufficiently. This work proposes a reinforcement-learning method for selective knowledge transfer, where its reward scores each opportunity to transfer against supervised alternatives, so negative transfer is avoided and controlled during forward prediction instead of being diagnosed afterwards. Given limited data from a new target domain, the learned policy chooses among predictors based on individual source operations, subsets of the sources, or the supervised alternatives: fully pooled sources, or target data alone. A validation gate deploys the transferred prediction only when it improves upon the supervised alternatives. The method is designed for learning variables supporting carbon accounting, as well as performance and quality outcomes. We demonstrate the approach by quantifying the embodied greenhouse-gas emissions of parts produced via material-extrusion additive manufacturing, using data from 729 experiments spanning five materials: ABS, PETG, TPU, PLA, and recycled PLA. The response combines measured fabrication electricity with polymer-specific cradle-to-gate production factors, while 22 material, process, and toolpath features characterize each experiment. In leave-one-material-out evaluation, this method achieves a mean test RMSE of 5.2 g CO2e per part, 20.00% lower than target-only training (32.5% lower when only 5-10% of the target training data are available) and 10.30% lower than indiscriminate source-target pooling.

infographic.key_insight: A reinforcement-learning policy can decide when to reuse source-domain knowledge and when to rely on target data, reducing negative transfer for carbon-footprint prediction in new manufacturing domains.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables more reliable early-stage embodied-carbon estimates for new materials and processes in additive manufacturing, supporting faster design and sustainability decisions with limited target data.
method: Trains a selective transfer policy that compares source-based predictors against supervised alternatives.
Uses a validation gate to accept transferred predictions only when they outperform target-only or fully pooled models.
Applied to embodied GHG prediction for material-extrusion AM using 22 material, process, and toolpath features.
infographic.evidence_signal: On 729 experiments across five materials, leave-one-material-out testing achieved a mean RMSE of 5.2 g CO2e per part, outperforming target-only training by 20.00% and source-target pooling by 10.30%.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on having enough representative source domains and a reliable validation split; poorly matched source data can still limit transfer if the gating policy is not well calibrated.
infographic.paper_title: Learning When to Transfer: Reinforcement Learning for Carbon-Footprint Modeling in New Manufacturing Domains

title: Ionic gradients shape the spatial organization and dynamics of supramolecular polymers
authors: Claudio Perego, Annalisa Cardellini, Andrea Tagliabue, Giovanni M. Pavan
abstract: Living supramolecular materials such as microtubules and actin filaments assemble and function in dynamic, heterogeneous environments, subject to chemical concentration gradients. Their rapid and precise response to such gradients---via aggregation, disassembly, or autonomous motion---underlies the fine spatiotemporal control typical of living systems. Reproducing such responsiveness in synthetic materials is a central challenge in materials science and requires a molecular-level understanding of how gradients couple to supramolecular structure and dynamics, which remains difficult to access experimentally. To this end, we combine implicit-solvent coarse-grained molecular dynamics (MD) with the constant chemical potential MD (C$μ$MD) technique to investigate, at molecular resolution, the coupling of two prototypical supramolecular polymer models with externally imposed ionic concentration gradients. Despite their contrasting responses to homogeneous ionic conditions, both systems undergo pronounced spatial reorganization under the gradient, generating regions of locally enhanced supramolecular activity that are inaccessible to homogeneous systems with the same overall content of self-assembling species. Crucially, the local supramolecular dynamics is largely determined by the local concentrations, consistent with the formation of local quasi-equilibria: this direct connection between spatial composition and supramolecular activity emerges as a common governing principle across the two models. These findings shed light on the spatially complex supramolecular response that can be triggered by chemical gradients, and show how a single gradient simulation can encode this response across a continuous range of local chemical environments, thus providing a general strategy to investigate and design materials operating under spatially heterogeneous conditions.

infographic.key_insight: Ionic concentration gradients reorganize supramolecular polymers into spatial zones with locally enhanced assembly dynamics, and those local dynamics are largely governed by the local ionic environment rather than the global average composition.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This suggests chemical gradients can be used as a design handle to program where and how synthetic supramolecular materials assemble, adapt, or move in heterogeneous environments.
method: Implicit-solvent coarse-grained molecular dynamics
Constant chemical potential MD (CμMD) to impose ionic gradients
Comparison of two prototypical supramolecular polymer models under gradient vs homogeneous conditions
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports molecular-resolution simulation results showing pronounced spatial reorganization and local quasi-equilibria across two models, enabling a single gradient simulation to represent a continuum of local chemical environments.
infographic.watch_item: The conclusions are simulation-based and depend on coarse-grained/implicit-solvent assumptions, so experimental validation and parameter transferability should be checked before device-level deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Ionic gradients shape the spatial organization and dynamics of supramolecular polymers

title: Knowledge-Guided Construction of Machine Learning Potentials for Reactive Behavior in Energetic Materials
authors: Guanchen Dong, Huanrong Liu, Lin Wang, Yuxuan Chen, Zhengyu Tu, Qing-an Li
abstract: Energetic materials involve multiple interactions, making reliable machine-learning potentials (MLPs) difficult to construct without extensive datasets. Here, we enhance the ability of the neural network interatomic potential (NNAP) to describe molecular systems using sphmulti, a refined spherical-harmonic basis set that combines extra radial basis with element-specific chemical weighting in each radial channel. We further integrate hyperactive learning, farthest-point sampling, and iterative sufficiency criteria with knowledge-guided key events, enabling the NNAP to retain essential information for describing the material system. For 3,3'-diamino-4,4'-azoxyfurazan, the resulting NNAP is trained on only 13,680 configurations yet captures key properties, including the isomerization barrier, pyrolysis activation energy, and shock Hugoniot behavior. NNAP-driven molecular dynamics simulations further reveal that pyrolysis proceeds through furazan-ring opening followed by chain reactions, whereas shock loading induces anisotropic hydrogen transfer driven by interlayer structural deformations. This work enables efficient and reliable MLPs for energetic materials.

infographic.key_insight: A knowledge-guided neural network interatomic potential can achieve reliable reactive-energy predictions for energetic materials with far fewer training configurations by combining enriched basis functions, adaptive sampling, and key-event selection.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This approach lowers the data burden for building transferable machine-learning potentials that can support safer, faster prediction of pyrolysis, isomerization, and shock-response behavior in energetic materials.
method: Enhanced NNAP with sphmulti: extra radial basis plus element-specific chemical weighting in each radial channel.
Used hyperactive learning, farthest-point sampling, and iterative sufficiency criteria to retain important configurations.
Guided training with key events relevant to reactive pathways in 3,3'-diamino-4,4'-azoxyfurazan.
infographic.evidence_signal: The model was trained on only 13,680 configurations and reproduced the isomerization barrier, pyrolysis activation energy, and shock Hugoniot behavior.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may depend on careful selection of key events and sampling strategy, so transferring the workflow to other energetic systems could require re-tuning.
infographic.paper_title: Knowledge-Guided Construction of Machine Learning Potentials for Reactive Behavior in Energetic Materials

title: Trust-Limited Machine-Learning-Accelerated Nudged Elastic Band Calculations for Small-Polaron Hopping in Rutile TiO2
authors: Ashish Kumar Singh, Irina V. Lebedeva
abstract: Nudged elastic band (NEB) calculations of small-polaron hopping are demanding because nuclear motion is coupled to a self-consistent localized electronic state. Near the charge-transfer region, slow self-consistent-field convergence, localization switching, and competing electronic solutions complicate surrogate-assisted optimization. We develop a Gaussian-process-assisted NEB workflow for this regime and demonstrate electron small-polaron hopping in rutile TiO2 using spin-polarized density functional theory with a Hubbard U correction (DFT+U ) with SIESTA. A joint energy-force Gaussian process (GP) with a Matérn covariance model advances the elastic band, while active-atom root-mean-square and maximum-atom displacement limits constrain surrogate motion relative to evaluated configurations. Reaching these limits triggers first-principles sampling without requiring full surrogate convergence. Three independently DFT-verified 96-atom [001] calculations using 11, 13, and 15 images and different surrogate settings and GP parameterizations yield barriers of 0.1645, 0.1637, and 0.1640 eV, respectively, spanning 0.793 meV. In the 15-image calculation, repeated central-image sampling activates a separately calibrated local GP during surrogate optimization. Final full-band DFT verification gives a maximum projected NEB force of 0.0346 eV/Å. A 324-atom calculation yields a lower barrier of 0.1302 eV, indicating supercell sensitivity and demonstrating feasibility at larger GP observation dimension. The workflow combines controlled surrogate extrapolation, targeted charge-transfer-region interpolation, and independent DFT verification to obtain polaron migration pathways, emphasizing reproducible barriers and full-band force convergence.

infographic.key_insight: A trust-limited Gaussian-process surrogate can accelerate NEB calculations for small-polaron hopping while preserving DFT-level verification through controlled sampling and force limits.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables more practical computation of charge-transport barriers in correlated materials like TiO2, supporting faster screening of ionic/electronic migration pathways.
method: Joint energy-force Gaussian process with Matérn covariance guides NEB image updates
Active-atom RMS and max displacement trust limits trigger first-principles DFT resampling
Independent full-band DFT verification checks final pathway and barrier convergence
infographic.evidence_signal: Three independently verified 96-atom runs produced consistent barriers of 0.1637–0.1645 eV, with a final full-band maximum projected force of 0.0346 eV/Å.
infographic.watch_item: Barrier values changed in the larger 324-atom supercell, so results remain sensitive to supercell size and surrogate calibration near charge-transfer switching.
infographic.paper_title: Trust-Limited Machine-Learning-Accelerated Nudged Elastic Band Calculations for Small-Polaron Hopping in Rutile TiO2

title: Improved screening of doped ZrO$_2$ catalysts for CO$_2$ hydrogenation from graph-based machine learning
authors: Karsten Walz Jensen, Mie Andersen, Raffaele Cheula
abstract: Dopants can tune the activity of zirconia-based CO$_2$ hydrogenation catalysts through changes in adsorbate and transition-state (TS) energetics. Computing these quantities with density functional theory (DFT) becomes expensive when several dopants, reaction intermediates, and TSs must be screened. Here, we further develop the graph-based machine learning method Wasserstein Weisfeiler-Lehman Gaussian Process Regression (WWL-GPR): we introduce additional electronic-structure and local-environment features relevant for oxide surfaces and use the resulting model to predict adsorption and TS energies on ZrO$_2$(101) surfaces doped with Al$^{3+}$, Cd$^{2+}$, Ga$^{3+}$, In$^{3+}$, and Zn$^{2+}$. Adsorbate-surface structures are represented as attributed graphs that combine bonds connectivity and features. We benchmark WWL-GPR against thermodynamic scaling relations (TSR) for reaction intermediates and Bronsted-Evans-Polanyi relations (BEP) for TSs, and then propagate the predicted energies to microkinetic CH$_3$OH-yield estimates. WWL-GPR consistently improves the prediction of reaction intermediate energetics relative to linear scaling approaches and provides TS estimates that are competitive with BEP-based models. These improvements become especially relevant when the predicted energetics are propagated through the reaction network. Microkinetic calculations show that WWL-GPR-derived energies give CH$_3$OH yields closer to DFT-derived yields than the linear-relation workflow. Degree-of-rate-control analysis links the activity errors to dopant-dependent rate-controlling steps, including HCOO* formation, H$_2$COOH* dissociation, and H$_3$CO* formation. These results support WWL-GPR as a data-efficient surrogate for connecting atomistic energetics with catalyst-screening observables on doped oxide surfaces.

infographic.key_insight: A graph-based machine-learning surrogate (WWL-GPR) predicts adsorption and transition-state energies on doped ZrO2 surfaces more accurately than linear scaling approaches, improving downstream CO2 hydrogenation yield estimates.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a data-efficient screening tool for rapidly ranking dopants in oxide catalysts, reducing the need for expensive DFT calculations in catalyst design workflows.
method: Represent adsorbate-surface structures as attributed graphs with connectivity plus electronic/local-environment features.
Train WWL-GPR models to predict intermediate adsorption energies and transition-state barriers on ZrO2(101) doped with Al, Cd, Ga, In, and Zn.

infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that WWL-GPR consistently outperforms thermodynamic scaling for intermediates and gives TS predictions competitive with BEP, with microkinetic CH3OH yields closer to DFT than the linear-relation workflow.
infographic.watch_item: Performance is tied to the available dopant/structure space and may be less reliable when extrapolating to chemistries or surface motifs outside the training regime.
infographic.paper_title: Improved screening of doped ZrO$_2$ catalysts for CO$_2$ hydrogenation from graph-based machine learning

title: PXRD-Bench: How Close Are We to Determining Crystal Structures from Powder Diffraction?
authors: Dongyeop Woo, Nofit Segal, Nayoung Kim, Minkyu Kim, Rafael Gomez-Bombarelli, Sungsoo Ahn
abstract: Determining crystal structures from powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) would enable routine characterization of newly synthesized materials, including those absent from reference databases. Generative models offer a promising approach, but existing evaluations remain fragmented and largely assume single-phase samples with known composition. To fill this gap, we introduce PXRD-Bench, a unified benchmark that extends evaluation to unknown per-element atom counts and recovery of both structures in two-phase mixtures. It provides approximately 4.1 million training structures with simulated PXRD, tests generalization to unseen compositions and structural prototypes, and evaluates recovery from experimental PXRD after excluding structurally matching training entries. To provide a strong reference baseline, we also introduce Bragglite, a PXRD-to-structure model developed through a systematic study of PXRD modeling choices. It achieves a 44.2\% Top-1 match rate on experimental RRUFF patterns with known composition, 24.6\% above the strongest prior baseline. Further analysis yields several key findings: some models fail to benefit from experimental PXRD, while generalization to unseen structural prototypes and recovery from two-phase mixtures remain challenging. Together, our benchmark, systematic studies, and Bragglite clarify the capabilities and limitations of current PXRD-to-structure models.

infographic.key_insight: PXRD-Bench shows that PXRD-to-structure models are improving, but robust structure recovery still breaks down on unseen chemistries, new prototypes, and two-phase mixtures.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This benchmark moves PXRD analysis closer to routine materials characterization by testing whether models can infer crystal structures from realistic experimental diffraction data, not just idealized single-phase cases.
method: Built PXRD-Bench with ~4.1M simulated training structures.
Evaluated generalization to unseen compositions, unseen structural prototypes, and two-phase mixtures.
Introduced Bragglite as a strong PXRD-to-structure baseline and systematically studied PXRD modeling choices.
infographic.evidence_signal: Bragglite reached 44.2% Top-1 match on experimental RRUFF patterns with known composition, 24.6 percentage points above the previous best baseline, while harder benchmark settings remained challenging.
infographic.watch_item: Performance on experimental data may not transfer reliably to unseen prototypes or mixed-phase samples, so benchmark gains should be interpreted cautiously for real-world deployment.
infographic.paper_title: PXRD-Bench: How Close Are We to Determining Crystal Structures from Powder Diffraction?

title: Role of defect trapping in the enhanced corrosion resistance of Ni-Mo alloys with yttrium and yttrium oxide additions
authors: Jia-Hong Ke, Xinchang Zhang, Jingfan Yang, Qiufeng Yang, Ruchi Gakhar, Rongjie Song
abstract: Corrosion of structural alloys remains a critical challenge for advanced molten salt reactors, where aggressive fluoride salts promote continuous dissolution at the salt-metal interface. While most mitigation strategies emphasize thermodynamic stability, kinetic control of atomic transport has received comparatively less attention. Here, we propose a corrosion mitigation strategy based on diffusion control and vacancy trapping by dilute yttrium (Y) solutes and yttrium oxide (Y$_2$O$_3$) dispersions in Ni alloys. A combined computational and experimental approach integrates density functional theory (DFT), self-consistent mean-field (SCMF) diffusion modeling, and an impurity trapping model to quantify the impact of defect trapping on effective vacancy mobility. Strong first-nearest-neighbor vacancy-Y binding, off-lattice vacancy configurations, and elevated rotational and dissociation barriers result in pronounced suppression of vacancy diffusivity, while Y$_2$O$_3$-associated sites treated as fixed traps in the model further reduce the mobile vacancy population. Ni-Mo (NM), Y-modified (NMY), and Y$_2$O$_3$-containing (NMYO) alloys were tested in molten fluoride salt at 750°C. Corrosion penetration decreases systematically from NM to NMY to NMYO, consistent with the predicted reduction in vacancy-mediated transport. The same trend is observed in mass change, with net weight loss decreasing from 0.52% for NM to 0.23% for NMY and 0.09% for NMYO. These results are consistent with an alloy-side transport contribution from defect trapping and reduced atomic transport. This study therefore suggests point defect engineering as a promising alloy design strategy for extreme nuclear environments.

infographic.key_insight: Dilute yttrium solutes and Y2O3 dispersions trap vacancies in Ni-Mo alloys, suppressing defect mobility and thereby improving resistance to molten-salt corrosion.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Point-defect engineering offers a practical alloy-design route for extending structural material lifetime in aggressive fluoride-salt environments such as advanced molten salt reactors.
method: DFT calculated vacancy–Y binding and migration barriers.
SCMF diffusion and impurity-trapping models estimated effective vacancy transport.
Corrosion tests compared NM, NMY, and NMYO alloys in molten fluoride salt at 750°C.
infographic.evidence_signal: The corrosion ranking matched the transport model: weight loss dropped from 0.52% for NM to 0.23% for NMY and 0.09% for NMYO, with penetration decreasing in the same order.
infographic.watch_item: The benefit depends on stable, well-dispersed Y/Y2O3 trap sites; performance may change if microstructure, trap density, or operating conditions differ from the tested state.
infographic.paper_title: Role of defect trapping in the enhanced corrosion resistance of Ni-Mo alloys with yttrium and yttrium oxide additions

title: Direct growth of crystalline spinel GaON films: A wide-bandgap mixed-anion semiconductor
authors: Baikui Li, Zecheng Yang, Wenhao Yin, Zijing Wu, Haitao Zhao, Yunwei Sheng
abstract: Mixed-anion semiconductors offer opportunities for bandgap engineering beyond conventional multication alloys, but competing phases and disorder complicate their synthesis and the identification of their electronic properties. Gallium oxynitride (GaON) could connect the technologically important GaN and Ga2O3 systems, yet establishing a clear relation between its crystal structure, composition and bandgap remains challenging. Here we report the direct growth of crystalline spinel gamma-GaON films by nitrogen-plasma-assisted pulsed-laser deposition. Varying the nitrogen and oxygen supply yields monoclinic beta-Ga2O3, predominantly disordered films and crystalline spinel GaON. Complementary diffraction, atomic-resolution microscopy and elemental analysis establish the spinel structure and nitrogen incorporation. Temperature-dependent photocurrent spectroscopy reveals a clear redshift of the crystalline gamma-GaON response, supporting assignment of a band-edge transition near 4.3 eV at room temperature. These results open opportunities to investigate mixed-anion wide-bandgap semiconductor physics and develop heterostructures.

infographic.key_insight: By tuning oxygen and nitrogen supply during pulsed-laser deposition, the authors directly grow crystalline spinel γ-GaON films and link this structure to a room-temperature band edge near 4.3 eV.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This work expands wide-bandgap semiconductor design beyond cation alloys, offering a new mixed-anion material platform for UV optoelectronics and heterostructures.
method: Nitrogen-plasma-assisted pulsed-laser deposition of GaON films with varied N/O supply.
Structural confirmation using diffraction and atomic-resolution microscopy.
Elemental/composition analysis plus temperature-dependent photocurrent spectroscopy.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that diffraction, microscopy, and elemental analysis verify the spinel structure and nitrogen incorporation, while photocurrent spectroscopy shows a clear redshift consistent with a ~4.3 eV band-edge transition.
infographic.watch_item: Mixed-anion films can be sensitive to competing phases and disorder, so composition control and phase purity remain critical for reproducible properties.
infographic.paper_title: Direct growth of crystalline spinel GaON films: A wide-bandgap mixed-anion semiconductor

title: Autonomous Science Bench: Evaluating AI Agents for Autonomous Scientific Discovery
authors: Yibo Wen, Han Liu
abstract: AI agents for autonomous scientific discovery must decide which experiments to run under a limited budget. Most benchmarks for science agents provide fixed datasets, while others that support active experimentation largely rely on simulation. We introduce Autonomous Science Bench, an initial release comprising six budgeted design-build-test-learn campaigns grounded in published experiments across biology, chemistry, and materials science. Agents select batches of designs, receive measurements from a lab service, and use the results to guide subsequent experiments before delivering a predictive model. Success requires passing two calibrated gates: a discovery gate, which evaluates the designs the agent measured, and a learning gate, which evaluates its model's ranking of held-out designs. In a pilot evaluation of eight agent-model configurations and 144 trials, the best configuration succeeds in 67% of trials, while the hardest campaign is solved in only three of 24 attempts. The two gates reveal different weaknesses: some agents build accurate rankings but find too few promising designs, while others find promising designs but fail to predict which unseen designs will perform well. These differences are obscured by overall success rates alone. We release version 0.1 of the campaigns, lab runtime, and public leaderboard at https://yibow.me/autonomous-science-bench.

infographic.key_insight: Autonomous Science Bench tests whether AI agents can choose experiments, learn from limited lab feedback, and deliver useful scientific models under a strict budget.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For materials discovery workflows, the benchmark helps distinguish agents that explore well from those that generalize well, which is critical for efficient autonomous experimentation.
method: Six budgeted design-build-test-learn campaigns based on published biology, chemistry, and materials experiments
Agents pick batches of designs and receive measurements from a lab service over multiple rounds
Performance is judged by two gates: discovery on measured designs and learning on held-out design ranking
infographic.evidence_signal: In 144 pilot trials across eight agent-model configurations, the best setup succeeded in 67% of trials, while the hardest campaign was solved only 3 times out of 24 attempts.
infographic.watch_item: Because the benchmark is currently version 0.1 and based on a limited set of six campaigns, results may not fully generalize to all autonomous discovery settings.
infographic.paper_title: Autonomous Science Bench: Evaluating AI Agents for Autonomous Scientific Discovery

title: Collision Cascade Morphology and Defect Nucleation in Pure Tungsten and an Equimolar Refractory W-Ta-Cr-V Alloy
authors: Mark Fedorov, Francisco Javier Dominguez-Gutierrez
abstract: Collision cascades and defect-formation mechanisms in pure W and the WTaCrV refractory high-entropy alloy were investigated using molecular dynamics simulations over primary knock-on atom (PKA) energies of 0.1-100 keV. Machine-learning tabulated Gaussian approximation potentials (tabGAP), complemented by short-range Ziegler-Biersack-Littmark (ZBL) interactions, were employed. Analysis of the heat spike lifetime, affected region, atomic relocations and surviving defects reveals an importance of subcascade formation and presence of light elements in the alloy. Cascade splitting into subcascades contributes to the distribution of the PKA energy over a larger region in the material, nucleating less dislocations and smaller voids - latter being present only in W and absent in WTaCrV. Since cascade splitting is more frequently observed in WTaCrV, the alloy shows better resistance to primary irradiation damage compared to pure W. Apart from cascade splitting, analysis of interstitials shows that Cr and to lesser extent V, being lighter and smaller elements, accommodate the damage in form of point defects, contributing to the mitigation of formation of the dislocation loops.

infographic.key_insight: In WTaCrV, collision cascades split into subcascades more often than in pure W, spreading energy over a larger volume and reducing severe defect formation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This suggests equimolar refractory alloys can offer improved radiation tolerance for fusion and other high-dose environments compared with pure tungsten.
method: Molecular dynamics simulations across 0.1–100 keV PKA energies
Machine-learning tabGAP interatomic potential with short-range ZBL repulsion
Compared cascade morphology, atomic relocations, and surviving defects in pure W vs WTaCrV
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that WTaCrV shows more frequent cascade splitting, fewer dislocations, and no voids, while pure W forms smaller voids.
infographic.watch_item: The conclusions are based on atomistic simulations and may depend on the interatomic potential and the specific composition/irradiation conditions studied.
infographic.paper_title: Collision Cascade Morphology and Defect Nucleation in Pure Tungsten and an Equimolar Refractory W-Ta-Cr-V Alloy

title: Heterogeneous Agentic Coevolution
authors: Wenqian Ye, Ziwei Guan, Zi Yang, Shivani Modi, Cici Cong Wu, Yunlong He
abstract: Recent advances in self-improving LLM agents have demonstrated the potential of AI systems that drive their own intelligence. However, many domain-specific applications rely on specialized foundation models that possess strong domain expertise but remain dependent on human-designed improvements. Extending recursive self-improvement to these models presents a key challenge: as a specialist improves, the strategies used to advance it must also adapt. To address this challenge, we propose Heterogeneous Agentic CoEvolution (HACE), a framework that jointly evolves specialized foundation models and LLM agents through reciprocal learning. HACE improves the specialist through supervised learning while training the agent with on-policy reinforced self-training, guided by verified performance gains on the current specialist. The agent's exploration, in turn, informs subsequent specialist training, enabling both models to adapt to each other's progress. To sustain this reciprocal learning, HACE further employs evolutionary search to optimize their interaction harness, adapting how the models exchange information and select training experiences as their capabilities evolve. We evaluate HACE across three challenging domains: recommendation systems, protein function prediction in biology, and crystal stability prediction in material discovery. We show that HACE outperforms the evaluated self-improving methods on the primary task metrics across all three domains. These results shed light on heterogeneous coevolution as a universal approach to improving specialized foundation models through reciprocal interaction with a learning agent.

infographic.key_insight: Heterogeneous Agentic Coevolution (HACE) lets a specialist foundation model and an LLM agent improve each other through reciprocal learning, so both adapt as capability changes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For materials discovery, HACE offers a scalable way to upgrade crystal-stability predictors by coupling supervised specialist training with agent-driven exploration and adaptive interaction design.
method: Train the specialist model with supervised learning on improved experiences.
Train the agent with on-policy reinforced self-training using verified gains from the current specialist.
Use evolutionary search to adapt the interaction harness: how models share information and choose training examples.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports evaluation across three domains—recommendation systems, protein function prediction, and crystal stability prediction—and states HACE outperforms prior self-improving methods on the main task metrics in all three.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on a reliable verification signal and a well-tuned interaction harness, which may be costly or sensitive to domain-specific evaluation quality.
infographic.paper_title: Heterogeneous Agentic Coevolution

title: First-Principles Calculations of the Electron-Hole-Pair Creation Energy in Semiconductors and Dielectrics
authors: Dallin O. Nielsen, Massimo V. Fischetti
abstract: We present first-principles calculations of the electron-hole-pair creation energy in semiconductors and dielectrics, focusing in particular on AlN, 3C-SiC, 4H-SiC, Si, and SiO2. We have employed density functional theory (DFT) to calculate the band structure, density-functional perturbation theory to obtain the phonon dispersion, and time-dependent DFT (TDDFT) to calculate the electron energy loss function (via the dielectric function). We performed full-band Monte Carlo simulations of electron thermalization for energies up to ~100 eV and calculated the average energy required to excite an electron-hole pair. We calculated pair-creation energies of approximately 12.2, 6.5, 7.3, 3.10, and 16.7 eV/pair for AlN, 3C-SiC, 4H-SiC, Si, and SiO2, respectively. These values are in good agreement with measured data, with the largest discrepancy being that of Si (about 14.9% lower than the accepted experimental value of ~3.6 eV/pair). To improve the agreement for Si, we used the GW approach and the Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE) to calculate the quasiparticle shifts of the electronic band structure and the dielectric function, respectively. Finally, using the GW/BSE data, we calculated a creation energy of ~3.50 eV/pair. We find that the marked improvement in the accuracy of the calculated creation energy, when using the GW/BSE approach, is primarily attributable to the slight decrease in the magnitude of the electron energy-loss function when using the GW/BSE approach for energies below ~10-15 eV. Overall, it is clear that the competition between phonon emission and ionization near the intersection of the phonon scattering and ionization rates is largely responsible for determining the value of the creation energy, with the other major factor being the location and shape of the plasmon peak in the energy-loss function.

infographic.key_insight: First-principles electronic-structure, phonon, and loss-function calculations can predict electron-hole-pair creation energy in semiconductors and dielectrics, with the balance between phonon emission and ionization setting the final value.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These creation energies help model radiation response, carrier thermalization, and breakdown-related behavior in device materials such as Si, SiC, AlN, and SiO2.
method: DFT for band structures
DFPT for phonon dispersion
TDDFT plus full-band Monte Carlo for energy-loss and thermalization; GW/BSE refinement for Si
infographic.evidence_signal: Predicted pair-creation energies were ~12.2 eV (AlN), 6.5 eV (3C-SiC), 7.3 eV (4H-SiC), 3.10 eV (Si), and 16.7 eV (SiO2), with GW/BSE improving Si to ~3.50 eV/pair and reducing the discrepancy to experiment.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy depends on high-fidelity quasiparticle and dielectric calculations, and the results can be sensitive to the low-energy loss function and the assumed competition between phonon scattering and ionization.
infographic.paper_title: First-Principles Calculations of the Electron-Hole-Pair Creation Energy in Semiconductors and Dielectrics

title: Deep Learning-based Mechanical Characterization of Synthetically Generated Plant Fibers under Transverse Compression
authors: Nikolaos Kegkeroglou, Bilal Sabillah, Myrto Inglezou, Vincent Placet, Céndric Clevy, Antonios Porichis
abstract: Plant fibers are increasingly used as sustainable reinforcements in composites, but the intrinsic variability of their microstructure causes substantial scatter in transverse mechanical behavior, complicating composite design. Characterizing this behavior relies on finite element (FE) simulations requiring several minutes of high-performance computing per fiber, making high-throughput characterization across realistic fiber populations impractical. In this study, we propose a deep learning framework replacing this FE bottleneck with a fast pipeline. It includes two coupled recursive U-Nets predicting the step-by-step evolution of fiber deformation and internal stress fields under transverse compression, followed by a regression CNN estimating the transverse Young's modulus from the final stress field. Unlike prior approaches predicting stress fields for fixed configurations or idealized geometries, our framework recursively resolves the full temporal stress evolution for synthetic fibers derived from real hemp cross-sections, with or without a lumen. Trained on 1,000 synthetic fiber geometries with FE ground truth, it reproduces the stress field sequence with a Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM) of $0.9574 \pm 0.0074$ and a Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) of $0.0345 \pm 0.0079$. It estimates transverse Young's modulus with an $R^2$ of $0.938 \pm 0.024$, a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of $24.31 \pm 1.23$ MPa, and a Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) of $5.25 \pm 0.91\%$. Inference requires under one second per fiber versus five minutes per FE simulation, drastically reducing computational cost. This offers a fast, reliable tool for mechanical characterization of synthetic plant fibers, with promising applications in designing natural fiber-reinforced composites.

infographic.key_insight: A recursive deep learning pipeline can replace slow finite-element simulation to predict the transverse compression response and modulus of synthetic plant fibers from their cross-sections.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables high-throughput screening of natural-fiber reinforcements, helping engineers design more reliable bio-based composites despite large microstructural variability.
method: Generate 1,000 synthetic hemp-like fiber geometries, including cases with and without a lumen.
Use two coupled recursive U-Nets to predict the stepwise evolution of deformation and internal stress under transverse compression.
Feed the final stress field into a regression CNN to estimate transverse Young's modulus.
infographic.evidence_signal: Against FE ground truth, the model achieved SSIM 0.9574 ± 0.0074 and RMSE 0.0345 ± 0.0079 for stress-field evolution, and predicted modulus with R² = 0.938 ± 0.024, MAE = 24.31 ± 1.23 MPa, and MAPE = 5.25 ± 0.91%, while inference took under one second per fiber versus about five minutes for FE.
infographic.watch_item: Performance is demonstrated on synthetically generated fibers trained against FE data, so real-world transfer to experimental microstructures and out-of-distribution geometries still needs validation.
infographic.paper_title: Deep Learning-based Mechanical Characterization of Synthetically Generated Plant Fibers under Transverse Compression

title: High-throughput screening of Heusler alloys for thermoelectrics combining machine-learned densities of states and first-principles transport
authors: Shivam Randive, Ayana Ghosh, Rahul Dixit, Himanshu Pandey
abstract: Thermoelectrics turn waste heat into electricity, but finding new ones requires transport calculations too costly for whole databases. Searches therefore choose what to calculate from the electronic density of states (DOS), increasingly predicted by machine learning, yet such choices are rarely tested. We test them on all 106,235 Heusler structures in the DXMag database, screening 51,257 on density-functional spectra and 54,978 on neural-network predictions, and judging both by 3,625 band-structure and transport calculations. A DOS-derived Seebeck indicator ranks most compounds passing every transport and stability test within the top 1% of their population, and ten of the eleven established half-Heusler thermoelectrics calculated pass. Predicted spectra lose most band gaps, unnoticed by spectral-similarity metrics, yet still rank passing compounds near the top. The screen certifies 80 computational candidates, 61 without reported measurements. Computed or predicted, the DOS can choose what to calculate; only a band structure shows whether a gap exists.

infographic.key_insight: Machine-learned or computed density of states can effectively triage Heusler alloys for thermoelectric potential, but only explicit band-structure checks reliably confirm whether a useful gap exists.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This workflow enables much faster discovery of thermoelectric candidates by reducing expensive transport calculations while still recovering many known high-performing half-Heuslers.
method: Screened 106,235 Heusler structures from DXMag.
Used DOS from both DFT spectra and neural-network predictions to prioritize compounds for transport calculations.
Validated screening quality with 3,625 band-structure and transport calculations, then certified top candidates.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 51,257 DFT-based and 54,978 ML-based screenings, the DOS-derived Seebeck indicator ranked most compounds passing transport and stability tests within the top 1%, and 10 of 11 known half-Heusler thermoelectrics were recovered.
infographic.watch_item: Spectral-similarity metrics can miss lost band gaps in predicted DOS, so screening should be paired with band-structure verification before claiming a viable thermoelectric gap.
infographic.paper_title: High-throughput screening of Heusler alloys for thermoelectrics combining machine-learned densities of states and first-principles transport
